source.title: An Accelerometer-Based Training Load Analysis to Assess Volleyball Performance

paper.citation: Sanders GJ, Boos B, Shipley F, Scheadler CM, Peacock CA. An Accelerometer-Based Training Load Analysis to Assess Volleyball Performance. Journal of Exercise and Nutrition. 2021;1(1). doi:10.53520/jen2018.1034.
paper.abstract: This prospective single-athlete observational study tracked one Division I female outside hitter across a competitive volleyball season. Practice and match activity were recorded with a Catapult microsensor, weekly approach-jump power was used as a neuromuscular-performance measure, and match statistics were compared with practice-load variables. Forward regression related selected acceleration, deceleration, and jump counts to weekly jump power, while high-intensity practice jumps and hitting percentage were compared between wins and losses.
paper.tldr: A season-long case study found strong within-sample associations among selected wearable-load variables, weekly approach-jump power, and match outcomes in one collegiate volleyball athlete. The analysis demonstrates a possible monitoring workflow, but the single athlete, many candidate predictors, and observational design make the estimates unsuitable as population thresholds or causal dose recommendations.
paper.methods: One 20.5-year-old Division I female outside hitter who remained in matches was monitored through practices and games. A Catapult microsensor quantified accelerations, decelerations, and jumps at multiple intensity bands. The athlete completed a weekly approach-jump test, match statistics were recorded, and forward linear regression selected load variables associated with weekly relative jump power. Practice loads and match statistics were also compared between subsequent wins and losses.
paper.findings: Selected acceleration, deceleration, and jump variables jointly explained 91.7% of the observed within-sample variation in weekly relative approach-jump power. High-intensity practice jumps were lower before wins than losses (49.6 ± 26.7 versus 69.2 ± 39.8), and hitting percentage was higher in wins (.266 ± .190 versus .130 ± .129). These associations occurred in one athlete and do not establish that changing jump volume would cause better performance.
paper.limitations: The study followed one athlete for one season, so it cannot establish population norms, universal alert thresholds, or effects across roles and competition levels. Forward selection from many candidate predictors creates substantial overfitting risk, and the reported 91.7% explained variation was not tested out of sample. Win-loss results are also influenced by teammates, opponents, tactics, schedule, and other unmeasured factors. The observational analysis cannot establish causation.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the paper as a model for individualized longitudinal monitoring rather than as a prescription to cap high-intensity jumps at a fixed value. Predefine a small set of meaningful load and performance variables, visualize their time order, interpret changes in the athlete's role and technical context, and require prospective or out-of-sample confirmation before treating an association as decision guidance.
paper.athleteDev: For volleyball performance monitoring, pair position-specific jump exposure with a repeatable approach-jump measure and contextual match information. Evaluate whether within-athlete trends are stable enough to inform training conversations, while avoiding direct transfer of this athlete's counts or regression coefficients to other athletes.
paper.rtp: The study did not evaluate injury rehabilitation or return to sport. Its single-athlete monitoring structure could inform how jump exposure and performance tests are displayed during reconditioning, but it supplies no clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-volleyball progression.
